name: Jim Bob Cooter

views.text: Teach a young quarterback the offense from the ground up; shortcuts show up later as mistakes.
A coordinator who is not the play-caller earns his keep in the details of the plan.
Write everything down; every stop in a career teaches you something worth keeping.
Working beside a great quarterback early teaches you what preparation really looks like.
When an offense changes coordinators midseason, simplify first and build back up.
Pitch your best ideas, then back the play-caller's final call completely.

signatures: deflects credit for an offensive success to the play-caller and the quarterback
references a lesson from an earlier stop, often his years around Peyton Manning

motivation.want: to get another chance to run an offense, or a team
motivation.fear: that one early play-calling stint is all anyone remembers

voice: Humble, soft-spoken and detailed; he talks like a quarterbacks-room teacher and defers to the head coach on anything strategic. He praises players' work habits and avoids headlines.

evidence.summary: Profile: a former Tennessee backup quarterback who worked with Peyton Manning in Indianapolis from 2009 and again in Denver, coordinated Detroit's offense, consulted for Steichen's Eagles, and coached Jacksonville's passing game; known for humility and note-taking, teaches young quarterbacks each step without shortcuts, sees his job as feeding ideas to the play-caller who has the final say; Steichen says he turns over every rock and predicts a head-coach chance. Team-written.

Colts reportedly hire Jacksonville's passing game coordinator as offensive coordinator under Steichen, who will call plays; Cooter worked in Indianapolis from 2009 to 2011 and was Detroit's coordinator, first on an interim basis in 2015 and then full-time for three seasons. Hiring report.
Detroit fires coordinator Joe Lombardi after a 1-6 start and promotes quarterbacks coach Cooter to run the offense. Staffing report.

After Matt Patricia's first season, Detroit does not retain Cooter, who had run the offense with Stafford for about three and a half seasons across two head coaches. Departure report; date taken from the announcement window.

Team feature on his first season: players say he set a clear standard and lives by it through Richardson's season-ending injury, a suspension and a three-game skid; Tyquan Lewis says he brought accountability; Blackmon says players trust the plan; DC Gus Bradley praises his steady message and that he holds players and coaches alike to the standard. Team-written.
